title.en: Charan, the Dancing-Girl Who Refused to Be Cast Aside

region.zh: 平安道與漢京（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story set in the reign of King Sung-jong (c. 1490); collected by Im Bang (1640-1718); English ed. James S. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales: Imps, Ghosts and Fairies (1913), tale 'Charan', eBook #51002

summary.en: Keydong, the gifted son of a governor, dances with the accomplished kisaeng Charan at his birthday feast, and for six years they are inseparable. Sent home to Seoul, he leaves her as a pair of worn shoes, then can bear it no longer and walks five hundred li through snow to find her taken up by the new governor's son. Disguised as a snow-sweeper he glimpses her once; she recognizes him and they flee together to a mountain village. There Charan buys him a stolen book of examination exercises and makes him study by candlelight until he wins first place in the royal examination, and the king orders her honoured as his lawful wife.
summary.zh: 神童奇童於生辰宴上與名妓佳蘭共舞，六年形影不離。返京後棄之如敝屣，旋又難捨，踏雪五百里往平安道尋她，而她已入新任之子幕中。喬裝掃雪僅得一瞥，佳蘭認出他，二人私奔入山。佳蘭售釵環購得試帖書，伴讀三載，終於殿試奪魁，王命立為正室。

sensitivity.note: Folk romance from Im Bang's collection; depicts kisaeng (dancing-girl) status issues of Joseon society.

passages.text: At the time of this story there was a famous dancing girl in Pyong-an whose name was Charan. She was very beautiful, sang and danced to the delight of all beholders, understood the classics and was acquainted with history; the brightest of all the geisha was she. The Governor's son, a gifted scholar of sixteen, was set to dance with her at his birthday feast, and from that day forth they became fast friends together, in a love such as had never been seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Charan' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the time came to part, Charan cried bitterly, but the son showed not the slightest sign of emotion. 'When she is before my eyes she is everything, but when the time comes to start for home she will be like a pair of worn shoes, set aside.' Yet in Seoul, thoughts of love possessed him; one moonlit winter night he stole from the monastery where he was preparing for the examination and set out for Pyong-an, a rich man's son walking five hundred li on blistered feet, begging as he went, till his face was worn and blackened like a goblin's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Charan' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Charan was not at home; her mother refused him coldly, for she was kept in the yamen of the new Governor's son. The scribe whose life Keydong's father had once pardoned took him in, and lent him a broom: mixed with the snow-sweepers he entered the inner court and caught one glimpse of her before she turned and shut the door. One look had told her who the sweeper was; she wept, and so won leave from her keeper to go home and offer sacrifice at her father's grave — and flew straight to Keydong. That night they gathered her clothing and treasures and fled while the city slept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Charan' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the hills they lived in a thatched hut; she sewed day and night and sold her jewels, and sent for a pack-peddler's great book of examination exercises. He studied by candlelight while she spun silk beside him, for two years. He took first place in the special examination held before the King; the Prime Minister, his father, recognized the handwriting of a son he had mourned as dead. The King heard the whole story and said the woman Charan was no common woman and no dancing-girl: 'Let her be raised to equal rank with her husband, and let her children and her children's children hold highest office in the realm.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Charan' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Chang To-ryong's Home among the Genii

region.zh: 智異山，全羅南道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story set in the reign of King Chung-jong (c. 1520); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Story of Chang To-ryong', eBook #51002

summary.en: A filthy beggar called Chang To-ryong haunts Bell Street in Seoul, yet the proud magician Chon U-chi dismounts and prostrates himself before him, ranking him first of the three spirit-men of Korea. Fifteen years the scholar who feeds him sees the beggar die and go out the Water Gate on a stretcher. Twenty years later, lost on Chi-i Mountain, the scholar wanders into a transfigured world of palace halls and jade windows, where a radiant host greets him: it is Chang To-ryong, exiled for a fault to the earth, now returned to the genii, whose dead body the scholar had pitied. After a celestial feast he is sent home; next year the citadel cannot be found, and the master lives to ninety without ever aging in spirit.
summary.zh: 張道齡者，漢京鐘樓街之丐者也。其人垢面蓬首，而術士全羽峙每見必下馬拜之，曰朝鮮三神人，張居其首。某文士施飯十五年，後見其死而舁出於水門。越二十年，文士迷路於智異山，誤入另一世界：宮殿連亙，玉牖生光，主人風姿煥然，自道即張道齡——昔因過謫居人間，今譴滿歸真；感文士葬屍之恩，設天廚相款。翌年重尋，惟見危峰絕壑而已。

sensitivity.note: Taoist immortal tale; the 'genii' (sŏn'in) cosmology is explained in Gale's headnotes.

passages.text: In the days of King Chung-jong there lived a beggar in Seoul whose face was extremely ugly and always dirty. He carried a bag over his shoulder and went about the streets begging, sleeping at night beside someone's gate. The far-famed magician Chon U-chi, whenever he met Chang, would dismount and prostrate himself most humbly, and seemed to regard Chang with the greatest of fear. 'There are only three spirit-men at present in Cho-sen, of whom the greatest is Chang To-ryong,' said Chon. 'People of the world do not know it, but I do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Story of Chang To-ryong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The literary man who fed him saw Chang's dead body carried off toward the Water Gate, and wept over it. Twenty years afterwards, journeying through South Chulla Province, he lost his way on Chi-i Mountain, and the scene changed and seemed strangely transfigured; he discovered himself in another world entirely, with beautiful palace buildings and attendants in official robes. A very wonderful person in shining garments greeted him: 'I am Chang To-ryong. Do you not know me?' The outlines of the face were there, but all the imperfections had gone, and only beauty remained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Story of Chang To-ryong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Chang said, 'There are four famous mountains in Korea in which the genii reside. This hill is one. In days gone by, for a fault of mine, I was exiled to earth, and in the time of my exile you treated me with marked kindness. When you saw my dead body your pity went out to me; I was not dead then, it was simply that my days of exile were ended and I was returning home.' A great feast was prepared, with food such as was never seen on earth and angelic beings who played on beautiful instruments; the windows of the guest pavilion were of jade and precious stones, and there was no night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Story of Chang To-ryong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When farewells were spoken, Chang said, 'This is not a place for you to stay long in; the ways differ of we genii and you men of the world.' The master withdrew, planted a stake to mark the entrance, and suddenly found himself in the old world with its dusty accompaniments. The year following he went again to find the citadel of the genii, but there were only mountain peaks and impassable ravines. As the years went by the master seemed to grow younger in spirit, and at last at the age of ninety he passed away without suffering; the beggar's face, he remembered, had never grown older, nor his dirty clothing ever worn out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Story of Chang To-ryong' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fox at the Hill Pagoda

region.zh: 平安監營後園（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story set in a governor's tenure in Pyong-an; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'A Story of the Fox', eBook #51002

summary.en: Yi Kwai, a minister's son studying in the Hill Pagoda of the Pyong-an yamen, is visited at midnight by a pretty young woman whom no one knows. Suspecting a fox or goblin, he catches her, swings her on his back and shouts for help — but the household sleeps. She bites him furiously at the nape of the neck; he lets go, she springs to the ground, escapes, and is seen no more. The long-lived fox, says the note, never becomes an angel but takes on metamorphoses and appears on earth in various forms.
summary.zh: 李瑰夜讀於監營山亭，有麗女無故入室，默立一隅。瑰疑其為狐妖，急負之於背，大呼家人；闔宅酣睡無應。女齧其頸，痛極釋手，妖脫身遁去，自是不復見。注云：狐壽久而通靈，能幻人形，惑世多端。

sensitivity.note: Kumiho (fox-woman) motif; core Korean shape-shifter tradition.

passages.text: Yi Kwai, son of a minister, accompanied his father the Governor of Pyong-an Province. In the rear garden of the official quarters was a pavilion called the Hill Pagoda, where Kwai often went at night to study. Once, when his companion had departed, the door opened suddenly and a young woman came in, neat, clean and very pretty — evidently a stranger, for there was no such person among the dancing-girls of the yamen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Story of the Fox' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He concluded that she was not a real woman but a fox or some kind of goblin. Suddenly he caught her, swung her onto his back and rushed out through the gate, shouting for his stepmother and the servants to come. It was midnight and all were asleep; no one replied. The woman, on his back, bit him furiously at the nape of the neck. Unable to stand the pain, he loosened his grasp; she jumped to the ground, made her escape and was seen no more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Story of the Fox' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Puk-chang Sees the Beating at Bird Pass

region.en: Bird Pass, Mun-kyong County, Kyong-sang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鳥嶺，聞慶（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story set c. 1500s; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer', eBook #51002

summary.en: Cheung Puk-chang, the seer who reads a book once and knows it forever, sits with his aunt and tells her exactly where her overdue servant is: crossing Bird Pass, being beaten with straw shoes by a gentleman whose dinner he rode past without dismounting. The aunt laughs, notes the day on the wall, and when the servant returns everything proves true even to the smallest detail — the gift of he-an pang-kwang, spiritual-eye distant vision.
summary.zh: 彭璧昌過目成誦、通曉天文地理，尤具千里眼之能。姑有僕逾期未歸，彭坐而言：『彼此刻正過鳥嶺，因不下馬衝撞用膳縣監，被草鞋撲面而笞。』姑筆之日於壁。僕歸，驗之，果如其言，纖毫不爽。

sensitivity.note: Episode of the larger Puk-chang cycle (cf. korean-wonder-tale); spiritual vision lore.

passages.text: Puk-chang went one day to visit his paternal aunt. She said to him, 'I had some harvesting to do in Yong-nam County, and sent a servant to see to it. His return is overdue and yet he does not come. I am afraid he has fallen in with thieves, or chanced on a fire or some other misfortune.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Puk-chang looked off apparently to the far south, and said, 'He is just now crossing the hill called Bird Pass in Mun-kyong County. Hallo! he is getting a beating just now from a passing yangban, but I see it is his own fault: the official was eating his dinner at the top of the hill when your servant rode by without dismounting, and the gentleman had his men arrest your man, pull him from his horse, and beat him over the face with their rough straw shoes.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The aunt made a note of the day on the wall, and when the servant returned she asked what day he had come over Bird Pass — it proved to be the day recorded. 'Did you get into trouble with a yangban there?' The servant gave a startled look, and told all that had happened; it was just as Puk-chang had given it, even to the smallest detail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Yun Se-pyong and the Magician Who Became a Beetle

region.zh: 漢京（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story set in the reign of King Chung-jong (c. 1520); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Yun Se-pyong, the Wizard', eBook #51002

summary.en: Yun Se-pyong, a military minister who learned Taoist magic from a stranger met on the road to Peking, lives apart from his family in dread; in winter he puts red-hot iron cleats under each arm. The charlatan magician Chon U-chi, who can imitate the master of a house to slip into the women's quarters, gives him a wide berth: 'I am a magician only; Yun is a God.' Warned that Yun will come to kill him, Chon metamorphoses into a beetle under an overturned crock — but a beautiful young woman comes calling for Chon, goads the jealous wife into smashing the crock, and turns into a bee that stings the beetle to death. The same day Yun bursts into tears: his sister in Chulla has just died, and he sends a servant of the gods with funeral supplies over ten days' journey and back before sunset.
summary.zh: 尹深坪得異人授道法，威震一門；冬以燒紅鐵鐙夾腋。妖術士全羽峙能幻主人形入內室，畏尹如神，自言『我只術士，尹乃神也』。聞尹將誅己，幻為甲蟲匿覆瓮之下。俄有美婦登門尋全，激其妒妻擊碎覆瓮，蟲現；婦化蜂，蟄蟲立斃，蜂自飛去。是日尹忽泣，云妹適死於全羅，遣神差賫賻儀往弔，十日程途，兩三時而返。

sensitivity.note: Taoist magic-duel tale; transformation motifs Buddhist/Taoist in origin per Gale's notes.

passages.text: Yun Se-pyong was a military man who rose to the rank of minister in the days of King Choong-jong. He learned the doctrine of magic from a passing stranger met on the way to Peking. He lived in a separate house, quite apart from the family, so greatly feared that even his wife and children dared not approach him. In winter he was seen to put iron cleats under each arm and to change them frequently; when they were put off they seemed to be red-hot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Yun Se-pyong, the Wizard' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was also a magician in Korea called Chon U-chi, so skilful that he could even simulate the form of the master of a house and go freely into the women's quarters. Chon heard of Yun and gave him a wide berth, saying, 'I am a magician only; Yun is a God.' Warned that Yun would come that afternoon to try to kill him, Chon metamorphosed himself into a beetle and crawled under a crock that stood overturned in the courtyard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Yun Se-pyong, the Wizard' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At evening a very beautiful young woman came asking for the master Chon, and the jealous wife, raging at what she took for a secret second wife, smashed the crock with a club. The beetle lay beneath it; the caller suddenly changed into a bee, flew at and stung the beetle, and Chon, metamorphosed back into his own form, fell over and died, and the bee flew away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Yun Se-pyong, the Wizard' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The same day Yun broke down in a fit of tears: his sister had just died in Chulla Province. He summoned from outside the gate a man wearing a horsehair cap and a soldier's uniform — a Kon-yun-no, servant of the gods — gave him a letter and funeral supplies, and before dark the messenger returned with the answer from the house of mourning, over ten days' journey from Seoul, in the space of two or three hours.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Yun Se-pyong, the Wizard' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wild-Cat Woman and the Roasted Chestnuts

region.zh: 漢城南門內（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of Kim Su-ik, magistrate of Quelpart (c. 1620s); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Wild-cat Woman', eBook #51002

summary.en: Studying late, Kim Su-ik sends his wife to roast the family's last seven or eight chestnuts. She brings them; he eats. Then the door opens and in comes the exact duplicate of his wife, with a basket of roasted chestnuts. Seizing one in each hand, Kim holds both women fast until dawn — when the one on his right tugs, struggles, falls to the floor and changes into a wild cat, escaping through the door. The writer notes that while foxes turning into women is told in Chinese novels, the wild cat's transformation is more wonderful still.
summary.zh: 金守一深夜攻書，命妻炒慄。妻去而食至；未幾門啟，復有一婦攜炒慄入，形貌與妻毫髮無異。金各執其一臂，至雞鳴不放。右手之婦掙扎墮地，化為山貓，奪門而遁。作者歎曰：狐化婦人事中國說部多有，山貓之變尤奇，莫測其理。

sensitivity.note: Animal-transformation lore; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The former magistrate of Quelpart, Kim Su-ik, lived inside the South Gate of Seoul. When he was young it was his habit to study Chinese daily until late at night. Once, feeling hungry, he called for his wife to bring him something to eat; the household had nothing but seven or eight chestnuts, so she went to the kitchen, made a fire and cooked them herself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Wild-cat Woman' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: She brought them in a handbasket, cooked and ready; Kim ate and enjoyed them much. Suddenly the door opened, and another person entered — the exact duplicate of his wife, with a basket in her hand and roasted chestnuts. Beneath the light the two women were perfect facsimiles of each other, looking back and forth in alarm: 'What's this that's happened? Who are you?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Wild-cat Woman' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kim took firm hold of each woman by the hand and held fast till the break of day. At last the cocks crew and the east began to lighten. The one whose right hand he held shook and tugged, fell to the floor, and suddenly changed into a wild cat. Kim let her go, and she made her escape through the door.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Wild-cat Woman' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fist-Headed Arrow against the Bully Priest

region.en: Big Horn Bridge, Ta-in County (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大尹郡大角橋（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story told as of 1640; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Ill-fated Priest', eBook #51002

summary.en: By Big Horn Bridge a scholar and his servants lie senseless: a proud, arrogant priest has beaten them all with his stick for failing to bow. A lean military man on a cadaverous pony arrives, tightens his girth, takes his bow and an arrow with a 'fist' head, gallops after the priest, shoots him through the chest, pierces both his hands with the sword, strings them and ties the body to his horse's tail: 'Now do with this fellow as you please.'
summary.zh: 大角橋畔，某書生主僕被一傲僧盡擊撲於地。適有瘦弱武人乘駑馬至，怒甚，曰『此獠久欲除之』。乃束帶取弓，以拳鏃箭追射，貫其胸；復以劍穿其雙手，以繩貫之，繫於馬尾而歸，曰：『此畜任君處置，吾去矣。』

sensitivity.note: Folk vigilante episode; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In 1640, journeying past Big Horn Bridge in Ta-in County, a scribe saw a scholar and his four or five servants lying senseless by the river side. They told how, while eating their noon meal, a proud Buddhist priest came by who refused to bow; one of the servants shouted at him, and the priest beat them all with his stick until they were completely worsted, scolding the scholar for not reprimanding his men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Ill-fated Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A military man about forty, poor in flesh, riding a cadaverous pony, asked the cause and was very angry: 'Yonder impudent priest, endowed with no end of brute force, has attacked my people and me.' 'Indeed,' said the stranger, 'I have been aware of him for a long time, and have decided to rid the earth of him.' He dismounted, tightened his girth, took his bow and an arrow that had a fist head, and made off at a gallop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Ill-fated Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He overtook the priest and, as the man looked back, let fly the arrow deep into his chest. He then dismounted, drew his sword, pierced the two hands of the priest, passed a string through them, tied him to his horse's tail, and came triumphantly back: 'Now do with this fellow as you please. I am going.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Ill-fated Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: To-jong and the Coming Tidal Wave

region.en: Fishing village on the East Sea shore (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 東海漁村（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of Master To-jong (Yi Chi-ham, c. 1500s); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Vision of the Holy Man', eBook #51002

summary.en: The prophet-magician To-jong sleeps in a fishing village where an i-in, a holy man, suddenly starts in terror: in two hours a tidal wave will engulf the whole village. The unbelieving householder is persuaded, goods and all, to climb the rear mountain; To-jong stops half-way, and the holy man tells him he will get a fright but live. At cock-crow the sea lifts its face and the waves climb the mountainside to touch his feet, engulfing the whole town; when daylight comes the waters recede, the holy man's house is found vacant, and To-jong begs in vain to become his disciple.
summary.zh: 土亭子李之菡客於海濱漁村，夜有異人駭曰：『兩時內海嘯至，全村皆沒。』屋主不信，異人勸其舉家登後山之巔。土亭止於半山。雞鳴時，海水驟漲，白浪排空，攀山而上，沒其足下，闔村蕩然。天明水退，欲師事異人，而其戶已空。

sensitivity.note: Tidal-wave prophecy tale; links to the flood/deluge cluster.

passages.text: Teacher To-jong was once a merchant, and in his merchandising went as far as the East Sea. One night he slept in a fishing village on the shore, where another stranger called who was said to be an i-in, or holy man. The three met and talked till late at night. The holy man looked out over the expanse of water, then suddenly gave a great start of terror: 'An awful thing is about to happen. In two hours or so there will be a tidal wave that will engulf this whole village.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Vision of the Holy Man' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The owner of the house would not believe it; but the holy man said, 'Even though you do not believe what I say, let us go up the face of the rear mountain. If my words fail we can only come down again.' The master took his family and a few light things and followed him up the hill. To-jong seated himself about half-way up, and the holy man told him, 'Others would never escape if they remained where you are, but you will simply get a fright and live through it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Vision of the Holy Man' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When cock-crow came, the sea suddenly lifted its face, overflowed its banks, and the waves came rolling up to the heavens, climbing the mountain-sides till they touched the feet of To-jong. The whole town on the seashore was engulfed; when daylight came the waters receded. To-jong bowed and asked to become the holy man's disciple, but next day the house he had pointed to was vacant, and there was no one there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Vision of the Holy Man' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Man of God Declares the Flood

region.zh: 五台山，江原道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story dated 1605 in the telling; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Visit of the Man of God', eBook #51002

summary.en: Before the greatest rain since the founding of the dynasty, a woodcutter on a Kang-won hillside sees an angel in golden armour descend from heaven on a white horse, carrying a spear, with a Buddhist priest following. The Man of God raises his spear and declares he will flood all the earth from such a point to such a point; the priest weeps and prays him to let the wrath fall on himself, until the sentence is lessened by more than half. Both depart through the upper air. The woodcutter flees with his family, and when the rain comes Mount Otai collapses, sinks into a vast lake, and all the inhabitants are destroyed — the woodcutter alone escaping.
summary.zh: 江原道樵夫遇金甲神人乘白馬持戟自天而降，其後隨一僧。神怒指四方曰：『自此至此，吾將盡沒其地與其民。』僧泣求以身當之，神乃減其罰過半。二神冉冉升天而去。樵夫舉家避之，果暴雨大作，五台山崩，陷為巨浸，居民盡沒，惟樵夫得脫。

sensitivity.note: Flood/deluge cluster story; parallels biblical flood-intercession and Chinese flood myths.

passages.text: In the seventh moon of 1605, before a great rain fell, such as had not been seen since the founding of the dynasty, a man of Kang-won Province was cutting wood on the hill-side. An angel in golden armour, riding on a white horse and carrying a spear, came down to him from heaven; his appearance was most dazzling, and a Buddhist priest carrying a staff came down in his train.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Visit of the Man of God' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Man of God stopped his horse and talked with the priest, very angry; he raised his spear and, pointing to the four winds, said, 'I shall flood all the earth from such a point to such a point, and destroy the inhabitants thereof.' The priest cried and prayed him to desist: 'This will mean utter destruction to mortals; please let thy wrath rest on me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Visit of the Man of God' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Man of God answered, 'I have lessened the punishment more than a half already on your account; I can do no more.' Though the priest prayed still, at last he submissively said, 'Thy will be done'; and both departed, passing away through the upper air into heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Visit of the Man of God' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The woodcutter went home in great haste, and with his wife and family made his escape; from that day the rain began to fall. Mount Otai collapsed, the earth beneath it sank until it became a vast lake, all the inhabitants were destroyed, and the woodcutter alone made his escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Visit of the Man of God' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Spirit-Master of Imsil

region.zh: 任實，全羅道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story dated 1654; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Literary Man of Imsil', eBook #51002

summary.en: A man of letters in Imsil claims two demon guards constantly at his bidding. He thrashes a chess partner who refuses to pay his forfeit with an unseen hand; he shouts into a bamboo grove to drive off the crowd of devils come out of a neighbouring witch-koot; and on a journey he calls out 'Let her go, let her go' to the mid-air — for that very night the daughter of a village house, snatched by a devil and carried down the main roadway, was stopped by a man who in fierce tones drove off the spirit, and she returned to life. The scholar laughs it off as a woman's haverings and dies eight years later.
summary.zh: 任實有一文士，自言有二神將供驅策。弈棋賴債者，被無形之手剝衣痛笞；鄰村巫堂作法，群魔散入竹藪，先生喝斥逐之。又途中向空呼曰『放她走』。是夜投宿之村，其家少女病亡復甦，自言魂為鬼曳至大路，遇一人厲聲逐鬼，乃得還魂；隔窗見之，即此君也。先生笑曰『婦人囈語耳』。八年後卒。

sensitivity.note: Shamanic koot (kut) ritual appears as lived background; no restriction on historical description.

passages.text: In the year 1654 there was a man of letters living in Imsil who claimed that he could control spirits, and that two demon guards were constantly at his bidding. Sitting at chess with a friend who refused to pay his fine in drink, the master turned his back and called out suddenly into the upper air some formula, as if giving a command: an unseen hand bared the man's body and administered such sounding blows that they left blue, seamy marks, till he yielded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Literary Man of Imsil' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another time, while a witch koot went forward in the adjoining village with drums and gongs, the master rushed to the bamboo grove behind the yamen and shouted as if to drive off furies. 'A crowd of devils have come from the koot,' said he, 'and are congregating in the grove of bamboos; if I do not drive them off trouble will follow in the town.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Literary Man of Imsil' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Journeying with a friend, he suddenly called out to the mid-air, 'Let her go, let her go, I say, or I'll have you punished severely.' That night the village house they applied to refused them at first — the daughter had fallen ill and died that very day, and after some time came to life again. 'A devil caught me and carried my soul off down the main roadway, where we met a man who in fierce tones drove off the spirit, and so I returned to life,' said the girl, who had looked out through the window chink and beheld the very man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Literary Man of Imsil' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The scholar laughed and said, 'Nonsense! Just a woman's haverings. How could I do such things?' He lived for seven or eight years more, and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Literary Man of Imsil' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Butterflies of the Kang-wha Soldier

region.zh: 江華島村邑（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the Manchu War era (1637); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Soldier of Kang-wha', eBook #51002

summary.en: A plain soldier of Kang-wha, chief man of his village, cheers his sulking wife in midwinter by taking coloured silk bits from her workbasket, muttering a prayer, and flinging them into the air: the room fills with dazzling butterflies. He opens his hand and they all fly into it, becoming silk again. In 1637, when Kang-wha falls before the Manchus and all the island flees crying for their lives, he sits undisturbed eating his meals — 'The barbarians will not touch this town; why do you run so?' — and while the whole island is devastated, his village escapes.
summary.zh: 江華島一老兵善召蝶之術。冬坐悶，妻妒而縫，乃取其篩中彩絲碎帛，喃喃祝之，撒於空中，滿室彩蝶飛舞，眩目奪神；復握之於拳，張手則仍為絲帛。丁丑（1637）虜騎陷島，闔島奔竄，兵獨安坐家中，笑曰『虜不犯此村，何奔為』。島既殘破，而其村獨完。

sensitivity.note: Taoist son-sul magic tale; references the 1637 Manchu sack of Kangwha as background.

passages.text: There was a soldier once of Kang-wha who was the chief man of his village, apparently without any gifts. One midwinter day his wife sat sewing in the inner room, overcome by jealousy; to cheer her he said, 'Would you like to see me make some butterflies?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Soldier of Kang-wha' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He took her workbasket, selected bits of silk of various colours, tucked them into his palm, closed his hand, repeated a prayer, and threw the handful into the air. Immediately beautiful butterflies filled the room, dazzling the eyes and shining in all the colours of the silk itself. A little later he opened his hand, held it up, and they all flew into it, becoming pieces of silk only.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Soldier of Kang-wha' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In 1637, when Kang-wha fell before the Manchus, all the people of the place fled crying for their lives, while the soldier remained undisturbed at his home. He laughed at the neighbours hurrying by: 'The barbarians will not touch this town; why do you run so?' Thus it turned out that, while the whole island was devastated, the soldier's village escaped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Soldier of Kang-wha' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Snake in the Flour Crock

region.zh: 衿川郡家宅（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the family of Ha Yun, Chief Justice (d. 1449); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Cursed by the Snake', eBook #51002

summary.en: In the old family seat of Prince Ha Yun a servant lifting the lid of a flour crock startles a huge snake from its depths. The master has the jar broken open; the awful serpent is killed with clubs, piled with wood and burned — and the vile fumes that fill the house kill every soul of the family, then everyone who enters. A mysterious fire later burns the remaining buildings; to this day the place is known as haunted, and no one ventures to build on it.
summary.zh: 河演相公金川舊第，僕啟麵甕，忽有大蛇自甕中出。眾僕擊殺之，積薪焚之，惡氣滿室，闔家並來弔者相繼暴亡，第遂廢。未幾無故自焚，僅存基址。至今人呼為凶宅，無敢構屋於其上者。

sensitivity.note: Haunted-place legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The old family seat of Prince Ha Yun was in the County of Keum-chon. He had placed in an upper room a large crock used to hold flour. One day a servant, wishing to get some flour, lifted the lid, when suddenly from the depths of it a huge snake made its appearance; the servant fell back in alarm and told the master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Cursed by the Snake' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The master sent his men and had the jar brought down and broken open, letting out a huge, awful-looking snake. Several of the servants joined in with clubs and killed the brute; they piled wood on it and set fire to the whole, and vile fumes arose that filled the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Cursed by the Snake' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the fumes all the people of the place died, leaving no one behind to represent the family; others who entered died also, so the place became cursed and was left in desolation. A little later a mysterious fire broke out and burnt up the remaining buildings. To this day the place is known as haunted, and no one ventures to build upon it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Cursed by the Snake' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Screen of Cotton Cloth in the Road

region.en: Main road out of Seoul, Manchu War (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京大路（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the Manchu invasion of 1636; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Man on the Road', eBook #51002

summary.en: Fleeing Seoul before the Manchu cavalry of 1636, a crowd of refugees meets a stranger sitting peacefully under a pine tree in the very roadway behind a screen of a few yards of cotton cloth. 'Why should you die? Sit down by me and see the barbarians go by.' The enemy ride past killing every one they meet — but pass the seated group without apparently seeing anything, all day till evening. A captured escapee later confirms that the army skirted great walls and precipitous rocks at that very spot: the few yards of cloth had been metamorphosed before the passers-by.
summary.zh: 丙子虜變，漢京士民奔逃，遇虜騎塞路，勢無可脫。忽見一異人坐於道中大松之下，前置布屏數尺，安然自若，曰：『何為必死？坐而觀虜過可也。』虜騎縱橫，見人輒殺，獨過其處如無物，終日乃已。後有逃虜營者言：彼處但見崇垣峭壁，人馬莫能近。蓋數尺之布，已化城垣矣。

sensitivity.note: War-magic tale from the Manchu invasion; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the Manchu War of 1636 the people of Seoul rushed off in crowds to make their escape. One party came suddenly upon a great force of the enemy, armed and mounted; the hills and valleys seemed full of them. In their perplexity they saw someone sitting peacefully in the main roadway under a pine tree, quite unconcerned, with a screen of several yards of cotton cloth hanging before him as if to shield him from the dust of the passing army.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man on the Road' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Why should you die, and why are you so frightened? Sit down by me and see the barbarians go by,' said the mysterious stranger. The cavalry of the enemy moved by in great numbers, killing every one they met; but when they reached the place where the magician sat, they went by without apparently seeing anything, and thus continued till the evening, the stranger and the people with him sitting the day through unharmed in the midst of the enemy's camp.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man on the Road' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The following day the party fell in with a man who had been captured but had escaped. 'When I followed the barbarian army, passing such and such a point, we skirted great walls and precipitous rocks, against which no one could move, and so we passed by.' Thus were the few yards of cotton cloth metamorphosed before the eyes of the passers-by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man on the Road' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Man Who Became a Skate

region.zh: 高城郡河畔（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story told to a magistrate of Ko-song County; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Old Man Who Became a Fish', eBook #51002

summary.en: At a magistrate's table a guest grows pale and weeps before a dish of skate soup: his father, nearly a hundred, taken with a burning fever, begged to be carried to the river bank. Left alone at his own furious insistence, the old man stripped and plunged into the water; his body was already half metamorphosed into a skate, then became a great flatfish that disported itself in the water with intense delight, looked back at his children, entered the deep sea, and did not appear again. On the edge of the stream they found his finger-nails and a tooth, buried them, and the family abstains from skate fish to this day.
summary.zh: 高城郡守宴客，客見鰩湯變色而泣。自言其父年近百，患熱疾如焚，必欲臨河。眾強扶至岸，父命子女退入林中伺之。俄而父已入水，半身已化為鰩；俄頃盡變，鼓鬣嬉游，回顧兒女，若不忍去，旋入深海不返。岸上惟得指甲與一齒，葬之。子孫至今不食鰩魚。

sensitivity.note: Transformation-into-fish tale with food taboo origin; etiological.

passages.text: A guest of the magistrate of Ko-song County twisted his features and refused the dish of skate soup, saying he was fasting from meat; his face grew very pale, and tears flowed from his eyes. He told a story never before told to a living soul: his father was nearly a hundred when one day he was taken down with a high fever, his body like a fiery furnace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man Who Became a Fish' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man begged to be carried to the bank of the river before the house, saying the clear flowing water cured his sickness, and then furiously ordered his children to go away into the wood and wait till he called them. They turned to look: the father had taken off his clothes and plunged into the muddied water, his body already half metamorphosed into a skate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man Who Became a Fish' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: All at once it became changed into a great flatfish that swam and plunged and disported itself in the water with intense delight. He looked back at them as though he could hardly bear to go, but a moment later he was off, entered the deep sea, and did not again appear. On the edge of the stream where he had changed his form they found his finger-nails and a tooth; these they buried, and as a family they all abstain from skate fish to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man Who Became a Fish' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Geomancer and the Pheasant that Could Not Fly

region.zh: 楊州郡松山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the geomancer Yi Eui-sin (c. 1600s); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Geomancer', eBook #51002

summary.en: The geomancer Yi Eui-sin traces the great Dragon Ridge from North Ham-kyong Province to a beautifully rounded end at Pine Mountain in Yang-ju — a perfect burial site. He gives it to a poor mourner who fed him, with the warning that in ten years the luck will run out and he should send for Yi So-pang in Seoul. Ten years later a rival geomancer warns the now-rich owner that a Kneeling Pheasant formation cannot kneel forever: within ten years it must fly. But Yi, come from the capital, shows the whole group of hills — Dog Hill behind, Falcon Hill above, Cat River in front — and laughs: how can the pheasant fly, with the dog, the falcon and the cat all around? From that day the Yis of Pine Hill became a great family.
summary.zh: 相地者李義臣自北關追龍脈至楊州松山，得一圓淨佳城，指授貧孝子葬親，且預言十年後運盡當再請。十年後果有客慫恿遷葬，謂此地乃『跪雞形』，久跪必飛。李自松京至，遍指群山：後有臥犬嶺，上有飛隼峰，前有捕貓川，笑曰：『犬、隼、貓三者環伺，雞安敢飛？』李氏自是遂為望族。

sensitivity.note: Pungsu (geomancy) tale; landscape read as animal forms is core Korean earth-lore.

passages.text: There was a geomancer once, Yi Eui-sin, who in seeking out a special mountain vein started with the Dragon Ridge in North Ham-kyong Province and traced it as far as Pine Mountain in Yang-ju County, where it stopped in a beautifully rounded end, forming a perfect site for burial. Wandering all day in the hills, hungry, he was given a dish of white gruel by a mourner in a small house beneath the hill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Geomancer' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yi showed him the end of the great vein he had just discovered, the spot for the grave and how to place its compass points. 'After possessing this site you will be greatly enriched, but in ten years you will have cause to arrange for another site. When that comes to pass please call for Yi So-pang, who lives in West School Ward, Seoul.' All his affairs prospered as the geomancer had foretold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Geomancer' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: After ten years a guest warned the master that the luck was gone: 'This hill is a Kneeling Pheasant formation. If the pheasant kneels too long it cannot endure it, so within a limited time it must fly.' Yi came from Seoul, and laughed at the visitor's partial view: 'Yonder is Dog Hill, yonder above is Falcon Hill, and the stream in front is Cat River. This is the whole group — the dog behind, the falcon just above, and the cat in front; how then can the pheasant fly? It dares not.' From that day forth the Yis of Pine Hill became a great and noted family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Geomancer' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Patriarch Who Became a Pig

region.zh: 承平府地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story told to Minister Kim Yu (c. 1620s); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Man Who Became a Pig', eBook #51002

summary.en: The son of a patriarch nearly one hundred years old comes secretly to Minister Kim Yu. His father had called his children about him, ordered the door closed for a siesta, and never called them back; peering through the chink they saw their father changed into a huge pig, which grunted and rushed to get out. Some sons counsel keeping it in the house, some a funeral; Kim Yu judges: since the metamorphosis has come, do not bury it before death; since it is no longer a human being, do not keep it in the house — carry it into the trackless depths of the mountains and let it go free. The son buries his father's clothes in sackcloth mourning and observes the day of metamorphosis as the day of sacrifice.
summary.zh: 承平府有翁年近百，忽命闔戶晝寢。子女夜窺之，見翁已化為大豕，吼聲撞門。或議畜之，或議葬之，其子走問金輦相公。相曰：『化形既成，未死不可葬；既非人形，不可留於家。宜舁入深山無人處縱之。』子如其言，服衰葬衣冠，以化形之日為忌辰。

sensitivity.note: Transformation tale with ritual ruling; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: A certain Minister of State, Kim Yu, had a relative in a far-distant part of the country, an old man aged nearly one hundred. His son came secretly to the Minister's office: 'My father, though very old, was a strong and hearty man. On a certain day he called us children to him and said, I wish to have a siesta, so now close the door and all of you go out of the room. Do not let any one venture in till I call you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man Who Became a Pig' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Till late at night there was neither call nor command. They looked through the chink, and lo, there was their father changed into a huge pig! Terrified, they opened the door, when the animal grunted and growled and made a rush to get out past them. Some sons said, keep the pig within doors and care for it; some said, have a funeral and bury it; so the son came to ask counsel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man Who Became a Pig' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Prince Kim thought it over and said, 'No such mysterious thing was ever heard of before; but since this metamorphosis has come about, you had better not bury it before death; and since it is not a human being any longer, it is not right to keep it in the house. Take it out and let it go free into the trackless depths of some mountainous country where no foot of man has ever trod.' The son accepted the counsel, donned sackcloth, mourned, buried his father's clothes for a funeral, and observed the day of metamorphosis as the day of sacrificial ceremony.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man Who Became a Pig' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Goblin Pair in the Tablet-Box

region.zh: 漢城南郊（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Old Woman Who Became a Goblin', eBook #51002

summary.en: A scholar's wife takes in an aged, smooth-faced beggar-woman to spin thread, where she does the work of eight women in a day — until she grows angry at cooling generosity and demands the husband for a partner. Refused, she returns with a decrepit old man; the two boldly clear out the ancestral tablet-box on the wall-shelf and disappear into it, voices only remaining. They send plague and sickness when displeased; the children sicken and die, the relatives who come to see catch the plague and die, and at last no one dares come near. Smoke from the chimney shows the wife still a prisoner — then the smoke ceases, and all know her end has come.
summary.zh: 漢城南有儒士之家，婦人留一老嫗在家紡績，一日之功抵八人。數日後嫗怒，求主翁為偶，不許；旋引一僂翁俱至，竟入堂取壁上神主匵，二者俱入匵中不見，惟聞其聲。稍不遂意，則降疫於其家，子女相繼夭亡，來弔之親亦染疫而死。日見炊煙，知婦尚存；數日煙絕，知其死矣。闔邑無敢問者。

sensitivity.note: Ghost-story with ancestral tablet motif; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: A Confucian scholar in the southern part of Seoul went out for a walk one day while his wife remained alone at home. There came by begging an old woman who looked like a Buddhist priestess, for while very old her face was not wrinkled. The wife took her in to pick cotton and spin thread; in one day she did more than eight ordinary women, and yet seemingly had plenty of time to spare.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Woman Who Became a Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: After five or six days the old woman grew angry and said, 'I am tired of living alone, and so I want your husband for my partner.' This being refused, she went off in a rage, but came back accompanied by a decrepit old man who looked like a Buddhist beggar. These two came boldly into the room, cleared out the things that were in the ancient tablet-box on the wall-shelf, and both disappeared into it, so that only their voices were heard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Woman Who Became a Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the scholar's wife failed in the least particular to please them, they sent plague and sickness after her, so that her children fell sick and died; relatives who came to see caught the plague, fell ill and died. Little by little no one dared come near the place. For a time smoke was seen coming out of the chimney daily, and the town-folk knew that the wife still lived; but after five or six days the smoke ceased, and they knew then that the woman's end had come. No one dared even to make inquiry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Woman Who Became a Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Grateful Ghost and the Examination Poem

region.zh: 漢京山路（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the Koryo dynasty era (918-1392); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Grateful Ghost', eBook #51002

summary.en: Riding to the capital examination at dusk, a scholar hears sneezing from a creeper by the roadside; digging beneath it he finds a dead man's skull full of earth, the roots through the nostrils. He washes it in clean water, wraps it in paper, reburrows it on the hillside and offers food and prayer. That night a white-haired scholar comes in a dream: he died out of season for sin in a former life, his posterity destroyed, and begs to requite the kindness. He recites, rhyme 'pong', the winning poem on 'Peaks and Spires of the Summer Clouds' — the examination subject, foretold exactly. The candidate writes it and becomes first in the honours of the occasion.
summary.zh: 高麗某舉子赴試，暮宿山中，聞灌木根下有嚏聲。掘之得髑髏，根穿其鼻，靈困而嚏。舉子洗以淨水，裹以紙，還瘞於山原，祭以酒食。夜夢白髮書生再拜謝曰：『前生獲譴，夭於非命，子孫滅絕，骸骨僅存。蒙君厚恩，無以為報。今歲試題為「夏雲峰」韻腳「逢」字，我已代擬一首，用之必魁。』果驗。

sensitivity.note: Ghost-gratitude tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the days of the Koryo Dynasty, when an examination was to be held, a certain scholar came from a far-distant part of the country. Once on his journey he heard a sneezing from among the creepers and bushes by the roadside, and ordered his servant to dig round it: they found a dead man's skull full of earth, the roots of the creeper passed through the nostrils, and the sneezing caused by the annoyance felt by the spirit from having the nose so discommoded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Grateful Ghost' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The candidate felt sorry, washed the skull in clean water, wrapped it in paper and reburied it on the hill-side, brought a table of food, offered sacrifice, and said a prayer. That night, in a dream, a scholar came to him, an old man with white hair, who bowed, thanked him, and said: 'On account of sin committed in a former life, I died out of season before I had fulfilled my days. My posterity, too, were all destroyed, my skull alone remaining. By good luck you and your kind heart took pity on me, buried me in a clean place and gave me food.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Grateful Ghost' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Your present journey is for the purpose of trying the official Examination, so I shall tell you beforehand what the form is to be, and the subject: character groups of fives, in couplets; the rhyme sound is pong, and the subject Peaks and Spires of the Summer Clouds. I have already composed one for you, which will undoubtedly win you the first place.' The man awakened from his dream, came up to Seoul; and behold, the subject was as foretold by the spirit. He wrote what had been given him, and became first in the honours of the occasion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Grateful Ghost' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Maiden Who Held a Sword instead of a Fan

region.zh: 宣川，平安道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the reign of King Se-jo (1455-1468); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Plucky Maiden', eBook #51002

summary.en: The all-powerful Governor Han Myong-hoi, feared like a tiger through Pyong-an, demands the beautiful daughter of the Deputy Prefect of Son-chon as his concubine. The daughter laughs at her father's terror, and when the Governor arrives — not in his official robes but dressed as a commoner — she stands before him holding not a fan but a sword: if he takes her as his real and true wife she will serve him with all her heart, but if as a concubine she will die on the spot. The mighty Han falls victim at once, goes through every form of true marriage, loves her above all others — and years later, when King Se-jo calls at the house, she prostrates herself and wins from the king's own hand the document that makes her a real wife, her children eligible for the highest office.
summary.zh: 權相韓明澮欲納宣川郡守之女為妾，郡守惶恐，女獨笑曰：『一女易一命，何憂。』及相至，女不執扇而執劍，曰：『納我為正室則終身奉事；以妾畜我則當日自刎。』相為之屈，遂以六禮聘焉。後王以布衣幸其家，女伏地泣訴，王親書判詞，許為正室，子孫得科第。

sensitivity.note: Tale of forced concubinage resisted; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: When Han went as governor to Pyong-an Province he did all manner of lawless things; the whole Province feared him as they would a tiger. Hearing that the Deputy Prefect of Son-chon had a very beautiful daughter, he called him: 'I would like to make her my concubine. When I am on my official rounds shortly, I shall expect to stop at your town and take her.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Plucky Maiden' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Deputy told his daughter in despair; she made light of it and laughed. 'Why should a grown man lose his life for the sake of a girl? A daughter does not count; give her over.' The girl alone seemed perfectly unmoved, not showing the slightest sign of fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Plucky Maiden' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Governor reached Son-chon he came not in his official robes but in the dress and hat of a commoner. In the inner quarters the daughter stood straight before him; her two hands were lifted in ceremonial form, but instead of holding a fan to hide her face she held a sword. Her nurse answered for her: 'If you take me as your real and true wife I'll serve you with all my heart, but if you are determined to take me as a concubine I shall die now by this sword. My life rests on one word from your Excellency.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Plucky Maiden' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Governor, though a man who never brooked a question, fell a victim to her at once and said, 'If you so decide, then I'll make you my real wife.' He carried out the forms to the letter, and they were married; he set aside his other wives and fixed his affections on her only. Years later King Se-jo, visiting in commoner's dress, heard her story, laughed, wrote out with his own hand a document making her a real wife and her children eligible for the highest office, signed it, stamped it and gave it to her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Plucky Maiden' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wife with the Decayed Meat

region.zh: 漢城王宮（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the tyrant King Yon-san's reign (1494-1506); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Resourceful Wife', eBook #51002

summary.en: In the last year of Yon-san terrible evils were abroad: the king ordered his eunuchs to bring him any beautiful woman they saw in the homes of the nobility, and no one escaped him. A young minister's wife, knowing she might be called at any moment, keeps two slices of decayed, foul-smelling meat constantly ready under her arms. Summoned to the palace, she comes without a tear; when King Yon-san orders her close, a most terrible odour arises — he holds his fan before his face, turns aside, spits, and has her taken away, and so she escapes undefiled. All who knew of it praised her bravery and sagacity.
summary.zh: 燕山君末年，暴政虐民，令閹宦強取士族美婦入宮，無得免者。有某相公媳婦，預藏腐肉二片於腋下。徵召之日至，眾婦哭別，獨此婦昂然入宮。王召至前，忽有異臭撲鼻，王掩扇唾曰『此婦不可近』，命逐出。婦遂完璧而歸。聞者皆歎其智勇。

sensitivity.note: Historical tyrant narrative; palace sexual coercion referenced but not depicted.

passages.text: In the last year of Yon-san terrible evils were abroad among the people. His Majesty gave orders to his eunuchs and underlings to bring to him any women of special beauty they might see in the homes of the highest nobility, and whoever pleased him he used as his own. 'Never mind objections,' said he, 'take them by force and come.' No one escaped him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Resourceful Wife' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A young wife of a certain minister was ordered into the Palace. Other women, when called, would cry and behave as though their lives were forfeited, but she showed not the slightest sign of fear. King Yon-san saw her and ordered her to come close, when suddenly the most terrible odour imaginable was noticeable. The King held his fan before his face, turned aside, spat, and said, 'Dear me, I cannot stand this one, take her away' — and so she escaped undefiled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Resourceful Wife' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: She knew she was likely to be called at any moment, and so had planned a ruse: two slices of meat, decayed and foul-smelling, constantly on hand, placed under her arms as she dressed. All that knew of it praised her bravery and sagacity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Resourceful Wife' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boxed-up Governor

region.zh: 慶州（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Boxed-up Governor', eBook #51002

summary.en: A sanctimonious Governor of Kyong-ju calls dancing-girls devils and ogres; the Mayor secretly promises a rich reward to any girl who can shame him. A mere child of the kisaeng agrees, plays the lonely 'sister' of the Governor's boy until the old man himself invites her in, swears he means marriage — then she lures him, alone at night, into her hut, hears a 'husband' thunder at the door, and bundles the half-dressed Governor into an empty rice-box. The 'husband' claims the box as bought with his silk, hauls it to court, and the Mayor orders it sawn in two — from within comes a cry of 'Save me!' The lid comes back and the Governor climbs out, nearly dying of shame, in a woman's green dress-coat turned inside out, and leaves Kyong-ju never to return.
summary.zh: 慶州監司口口聲聲罵妓為妖，牧使懸賞使妓羞之。一小妓偽為其僕之妹，日日過門。監司果惑，夜赴其家，甫敘寒溫，忽聞外有『丈夫』叩門大鬧。妓惶恐，藏監司於空米箱中。偽夫索箱，謂以己絹所買，遂擔箱訟於官。牧使佯驚，命鋸之，箱中忽呼『救命』。啟視，監司披髮跣足而出，滿堂哄笑，取婦人綠衣反穿而遁，慶州至今傳為笑柄。

sensitivity.note: Satire on hypocrisy; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: A certain literary official was Governor of the city of Kyong-ju, and whenever he visited the Mayor it was his custom, on seeing dancing-girls, to tap them on the head with his pipe: 'These girls are devils, ogres, goblins.' The Mayor detested his behaviour, and sent a secret message to the dancing-girls: if any of you can deceive this governor and put him to shame, I'll reward you richly. Among them one girl, a mere child, said she could.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Boxed-up Governor' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the dress of a common townswoman she used to go by the gateway of the Confucian Temple where the Governor lodged, calling his boy out — her 'brother' — until the Governor himself, one evening alone, invited her in, swore an oath that he meant marriage, and arranged to come quietly by night to her hut, disguised in a felt hat she sent by the boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Boxed-up Governor' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they talked and drank, a call was heard from outside, and she cried in alarm, 'That's the voice of my husband, who has come. For murder and arson he has no equal.' Rushing back into the room she cried, 'Your Excellency must escape' — and in such a little thatched hut there was no place for concealment but an empty rice-box. In his haste and deshabille the Governor was bundled into the box.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Boxed-up Governor' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'That's mine,' said the pretended husband, pointing at the box; the pair hauled it to the Mayor's court to have the ownership decided, and the Mayor, after hearing, said, 'Since you each have a half-share in its purchase, there is nothing for me to do but to divide it between you. Bring a saw.' As the servants began on the box, a cry came from within, 'Save me; oh, save me!' The lid came back and from the inner quarters there came forth a half-dressed man — the Governor himself, to the convulsions of laughter of the whole place. He slipped on a woman's green dress-coat turned inside out and made a dash for his quarters, leaving the place never to return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Boxed-up Governor' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The One-Legged Man and the Giant's Castle

region.en: Unknown island in southern seas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南海某島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Told as a survivor's tale on Quelpart's shore; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Man Who Lost His Legs', eBook #51002

summary.en: A merchant buying seaweed on Quelpart sees a legless old man drag himself to his boat. The man tells of a gale that drove his ship onto an island where a giant in a great castle caught one of the company, cooked him before their eyes and ate him, then slept roaring like thunder. A comrade stabbed out the giant's eyes; in the blind flailing the survivors each seized a pig or sheep on their backs and walked out past the groping hands, axed loose the boat the giant's kin had caught, and put to sea — where a storm wrecked them all and a horrible fish bit off the teller's legs. 'When I think of it still, my teeth are cold and my bones shiver. My Eight Lucky Stars are very bad, that's why it happened to me.'
summary.zh: 濟州販海藻者遇一無腿老人，自述其船為風漂至一島，見巨堡高牆，中有一偉人，黑面巨睛，聲若驢鳴，捕其同伴烹而啖之，飲酒酣睡，鼾聲如雷。同行者夜剜其目，眾各負一豕一羊負之出門，巨人捫之皆畜，遂得脫。海中復遇風，船碎人沒，老人攀木得生，而兩腿為怪魚所噬。言猶在耳，齒冷骨寒，自歎八字凶星所致。

sensitivity.note: Cannibal-giant folktale; graphic elements paraphrased at summary level.

passages.text: A merchant in Chong-ju who used to go to Quelpart to buy seaweed saw, when he drew up on the shore, a man shuffling along on the ground toward the boat: an old man without any legs, who said he had lost them on a trip when he was shipwrecked, and a great fish bit them off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man Who Lost His Legs' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'We were caught in a gale and driven till we touched on some island. Before us on the shore stood a high castle with a great gateway. In it was one man only, whose height was terrible to behold, and whose chest was many spans round; his face was black and his eyes large and rolling, his voice like the braying of a monster donkey. He fastened the gate, made a fire in the courtyard, rushed after us and caught a young lad, cooked him before our eyes and ate him. We were reduced to a state of horror, like fish in a pot, beyond all possible way of escape.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man Who Lost His Legs' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'When he had eaten his fill he drank from a jar and lay down and slept, his snorings like the roarings of thunder. One of us took a knife, and while the monster was drunk and asleep, stabbed his eyes out. In the blind flailing we each took a pig or sheep on the back and made straight for the gate; the monster felt each, and finding it a pig or a sheep let it go. Thus we all got out and rushed for the boat, axed loose the hands of the other giants who had caught it, and got free at last to the open sea.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man Who Lost His Legs' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Again a great wind arose, and we ran onto the rocks; every one was engulfed and drowned. I alone got hold of a piece of boat-timber and lived; then a horrible fish from the sea came swimming after me and bit off my legs. At last I drifted back home and here I am. When I think of it still, my teeth are cold and my bones shiver. My Eight Lucky Stars are very bad, that's why it happened to me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Man Who Lost His Legs' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Ten Thousand Devils at the New Year Roll-Call

region.zh: 忠清道韓公宅（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of Prince Han Chun-kyom (1579-1651 era); collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Ten Thousand Devils', eBook #51002

summary.en: Prince Han's poor, uncouth relative lingers past New Year and confesses he must call up all manner of evil genii at the season, run over their names and inspect them, or lose control altogether. In the scrubbed guest hall, demons come crushing in one after another till the court is filled, bowing as an old book of devil names is read against them like a government yamen roll-call. Two late-comers are paddled and canged for injecting smallpox and typhus to survive — and the master charges all of them, three times ordered and five times repeated: do not spread disease. He learned it, he says, from an old despised priest to whom alone he was kind, in a cave behind a mountain monastery; and the craft, he tells the prince, can be held only by the poor and despised.
summary.zh: 韓公之貧戚自言歲首必召群鬼、按名點視，否則失馭而疫癘橫行。遂於客堂召鬼，果見魔眾填庭，如官府點卯，鬼卒按籍唱名。有後至二人，一以散布天花、一以散布傷寒為生，被笞百、荷枷收監。主人三令五申『勿散疫』而後遣之。其術得自山中寺後石窟之老僧；且言此術惟貧賤者可持，公卿不可。

sensitivity.note: Disease-demon cosmology of Korean folk belief; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: A certain Prince Han had a distant relative who was an uncouth countryman living in extreme poverty. At New Year's Eve he announced, 'I am possessor of a peculiar kind of magic, by which I have under my control all manner of evil genii, and New Year is the season at which I call them up, run over their names, and inspect them. If I did not do so I should lose control altogether, and there would follow no end of trouble among mortals.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ten Thousand Devils' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: They scoured the floors of the central guest hall. A startling variety of demons came crushing in at the door, horrible in appearance and awesome of manner, lining up one after another till they filled the entire court, each bowing before the master, who drew out a book and began calling off the names, demon guards at the threshold repeating the call and checking off the names just as they do in a government yamen, from the second watch till the fifth of the morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ten Thousand Devils' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: One late-comer confessed he had been obliged, to find anything to live on, to inject smallpox into the home of a scholar in Yong-nam; another, who had climbed the wall, had inserted a little typhus into a family in Kyong-keui. The man rated them soundly, ordered a hundred blows with the paddle, the cangue, and prison; then, calling the others, he said three times and repeated five times, 'Do not spread disease! Do you understand?' — and dismissed them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ten Thousand Devils' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He told how, a poor student in a mountain monastery, he alone was kind to an old despised priest, who led him by night to a cave behind the monastery and gave him a great secret: a catalogue of devils with magic writing, and the laws that govern the spirit world. 'Your Excellency has great ability,' said he, 'but the possessor of this craft must be one poor and despised, and of no account. For you, a minister, it would never do.' The next day he left suddenly and returned no more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ten Thousand Devils' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Student Who Married into the Land of the Fairies

region.zh: 加平，江原道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story set in the reign of King In-jo; the family left in 1635 before the Manchu invasion; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Home of the Fairies', eBook #51002

summary.en: A young student of Ka-pyong, overtaken by rain in the Kang-won mountains, loses his servant and his horse to sudden death, and is led by a white-haired patriarch past pines and a stream with a marble bed to a palace of precious stones — the abode of the genii, where he is awaited, feasted on food never seen on earth, and married to the master's daughter. Two years of joy; he climbs the highest peak and sees the islands of the blessed with souls riding cranes, phoenixes and unicorns; she bears him two sons. Homesick, he visits his mother and finds the dead servant and horse restored — but he has not yet forgotten the seven things of earth: anger, sorrow, fear, ambition, hate and selfishness. A friend's household letter warns that next year the village will become fish and meat for the enemy; in 1635 the family sells out, follows the genie messenger with the two sons, and is never heard of again — the year following was the Manchu invasion.
summary.zh: 加平書生冒雨入山，僕馬俱斃，遇白髮神翁指路，入水晶之宮——仙人之境也。主人久待，天廚饗之，以女妻之，生二子。嘗登絕頂，見海上三神山，仙真騎鶴跨鳳往來其間。後思母歸家，所喪僕馬皆無恙而還。仙僕誡曰：『君在仙境數年，而七情未忘，故有淚。』未幾仙使送書至，云明歲此村當罹兵燹。乙亥（1635）舉家隨去，無復蹤跡；次年果虜亂。

sensitivity.note: Classic otherworld-marriage tale; parallels Urashima/immram type.

passages.text: In the days of King In-jo there was a student of Confucius who lived in Ka-pyong. Travelling in Kang-won Province he was overtaken by rain; his servant suddenly died, then the horse fell under him and died also. Weeping, he met an old man with very wonderful eyes and hair white as snow, who lifted his staff and pointed: 'There is a house yonder, just beyond those pines; follow that stream.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Home of the Fairies' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He came to a forest of huge pines and countless bamboos, a wide stream flowing over a marble flooring, and then a beautifully decorated house with a copy of the Book of Changes on a marble table and a jade brazier burning incense. The master of the place, in a green dress with a jade staff of nine sections, said, 'I am the master and have long waited for you... This is not the dusty world that you are accustomed to, but the abode of the genii.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Home of the Fairies' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I have a daughter who has arrived at a marriageable age, and I have been trying to find a son-in-law. Live here, then, and become my son-in-law.' The wedding was held in a Palace Beautiful with jade bells and sweet perfumes, and he became a sharer in the joys of the fairies; his wife led him up the highest peak to see the islands of the blessed, peopled with happy souls riding on cranes, phoenixes and unicorns, and she bore him two sons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Home of the Fairies' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day he wept for his poor old mother, and was given leave to visit her: at the gate stood a poor thin horse with a worn saddle — the dead horse and dead servant restored. The genie servant warned him, 'You have been for several years in the abode of the immortals, but you have not yet attained thereto, for you have not yet forgotten the seven things of earth: anger, sorrow, fear, ambition, hate and selfishness.' Three years later a servant brought his two sons and letters: 'Next year the place where you dwell will be destroyed and all the people will become fish and meat for the enemy; therefore follow this messenger and come, all of you.' In 1635 they sold out, bade farewell, and were never heard of again; the year following was the Manchu invasion, when the village was all destroyed. To this day young and old in Ka-pyong tell this story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Home of the Fairies' (1913); not verbatim.
